extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in film, culture, and climate-change storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating or creating films and stories about climate change that aim to engage audiences, persuade or inspire action, and avoid common cinematic pitfalls. Focus is on narrative, tone, characterization, and persuasive impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling storytelling / captivation
rubrics_metrics.description: “They do need to tell tales that are compelling enough to captivate audiences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about climate change must first grip and hold viewers — the piece praises cinematic works that remain in the mind (example: Roland Emmerich’s The Day After Tomorrow) and contrasts those that fail to provide a strong hook. A successful film should sustain interest beyond a single message or outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness that changes thinking and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should be “truthful enough to have an impact on how those audiences act and think.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond dramatics or rhetoric, a climate story should convey truths in ways that plausibly influence audience beliefs or behaviors. The film should not simply scream facts but present them in a way that leads to reflection and possible change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on relationship with the natural world
rubrics_metrics.description: “What climate change stories need to succeed is ... an emphasis on relationship.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intimate, Attenborough-like presentation to help audiences see animals, plants, and ecosystems as entities with whom we have personal relationships. The article cites Attenborough and Pope Francis’ Laudato Si’ as models for creating empathetic, relational engagement with nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatable characters and interpersonal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their relationships make them relatable and show us a version of ourselves that we hope, in similar situations, we would be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character relationships (family, community, efforts to help others) create identification. The Day After Tomorrow’s family-centered storyline is an example: invest in human bonds so viewers recognize themselves and their responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sermonizing or outraged screed that overwhelms storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The film “settles into an angry and rather familiar screed about human stupidity” and “McKay’s outrage completely overwhelms his gifts as a storyteller.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating volume of moral outrage as a substitute for craft. Effective climate stories should avoid simply shouting moral judgments; they should weave moral urgency into strong narrative structure rather than letting outrage drown character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid old tropes and provide an original hook
rubrics_metrics.description: The film is “one old trope after another, wheeled out wheezy and tired with no real hook to keep you watching.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific tropes to watch out for include the politically self-interested president, soulless morning-news banter reducing issues to spectacle, and the messianic tech guru as caricature. Seek fresh angles, surprising stakes, or new narrative devices instead of reusing stock types without development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t overinvest screen time in contested-belief debates
rubrics_metrics.description: “The energy given to such debate is itself another part of the problem, a time waster that allows people to feel like they’re doing something meaningful when in fact they’re accomplishing nothing relative to the crisis itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While depicting denial and misinformation has relevance, excessive focus on spectacle debates (comet/no-comet analogues to vaccines/masks arguments) can make the story about arguing rather than acting. Prefer dramatizing consequences and concrete responses over extended meta-debate scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer pathways to conversion, hope, or constructive change, not only condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Come-to-Jesus moments are of enormous value, but only if they promise that you actually do get to come to Jesus... meaningful conversion... will ... involve a confrontation with our sinfulness, but also an invitation to greater love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic climax or moral reckoning should include credible possibility for transformation or actionable hope; pure despair risks alienating or demoralizing audiences. Include invitations to empathy, sacrifice, or collective action alongside critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other genres and allegory to convey climate themes indirectly
rubrics_metrics.description: “They don’t necessarily have to be literally about climate issues; ‘The Walking Dead’ is far more a story about climate change than it is about zombies, and ‘Game of Thrones’ is as well.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory, genre fiction, dystopia, or fantasy can explore climate consequences and social dynamics effectively. Filmmakers can embed climate meanings in non-literal narratives to reach wider audiences and illuminate systemic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance satire/farce with humane storytelling and insight
rubrics_metrics.description: McKay’s prior films “brought together farce and cutting socio-political insight in often-brilliant ways,” but in this case the combination is unbalanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and farce can be powerful tools for critique (example models: The Big Short, Vice), but must be tethered to human stakes and coherent storytelling; otherwise satire becomes merely shrill and loses persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize characters rather than reducing them to caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the film’s portrayals: media figures, tech gurus, and politicians are presented as stock types (e.g., the president interested only in midterms; media focused on DiCaprio’s hotness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flattening people into single-issue caricatures; give even antagonistic or satirical figures complexity so the audience can understand motivations and the social dynamics at play, which increases emotional and moral engagement.
